data.title: Pediculosis — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pediculosis** (Infestations)_

**Q1. Name the lice that infest humans.**
- Pediculus humanus capitis (head louse), Pediculus humanus corporis (body louse), Pthirus pubis (crab/pubic louse)
- Obligate blood-sucking ectoparasites; wingless, dorsoventrally flattened, six legs with claws

**Q2. Describe the life cycle.**
- Egg (nit) cemented to the hair shaft close to scalp → hatches in 7–10 days → three nymph stages over ~9–12 days → adult lives ~30 days; female lays 5–10 eggs/day
- Lice die away from host in 1–2 days (head louse)

**Q3. Clinical features of pediculosis capitis.**
- Children (girls more), itching of scalp esp. occiput and behind ears, excoriations, secondary impetigo, occipital/cervical lymphadenopathy
- Nits: ovoid grey-white 0.8 mm, firmly attached, cannot be flicked off (unlike dandruff/hair casts)
- Heavy infestation: matted hair ('plica polonica'), id-like papular eruption on neck

**Q4. Differentiate nits from hair casts and dandruff.**
- Nits: eccentrically cemented oval structures on one side of hair, not movable
- Hair casts (pseudonits): tubular keratin sheaths encircling the hair, slide freely along the shaft
- Dandruff: loose flakes easily shaken off; also piedra (hard nodules — fungal), trichorrhexis nodosa, hair spray droplets

**Q5. Describe pediculosis corporis.**
- Body lice live in clothing seams, visit skin to feed — seen in poverty, homelessness, refugees, overcrowding
- Itching, excoriations, hyperpigmented thickened skin ('vagabond's disease'), maculae caeruleae
- Vector of epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), trench fever (Bartonella quintana), relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis)
- Treatment: hygiene and laundering of clothing at ≥60 °C — no need to treat the body usually

**Q6. Describe pediculosis pubis.**
- Sexually transmitted; pubic, perianal, axillary hair, beard, eyelashes (children — consider abuse)
- Itching, lice and nits at hair roots, maculae caeruleae (slate-blue macules from louse saliva on thighs and trunk)
- Screen for other STIs; treat partners

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Wet combing with a fine-toothed comb (most reliable to detect live lice)
- Dermoscopy: live nymphs, viable nits (oval with operculum) vs empty nits (translucent with flat cut end)
- Live louse = active infestation; nits >1 cm from scalp may be old

**Q8. Treatment of head lice.**
- Topical pediculicides — 2 applications 7–10 days apart (second kills newly hatched nymphs):
- Permethrin 1% cream rinse (10 min), dimeticone 4% (physical — no resistance; preferred where resistance is common), malathion 0.5%, ivermectin 0.5% lotion (single application), spinosad 0.9%, benzyl alcohol 5%, abametapir
- Oral ivermectin 400 µg/kg on days 1 and 8 for resistant cases (>15 kg)
- Wet combing every 3–4 days for 2 weeks; remove nits with fine comb/vinegar rinse; wash pillowcases, combs, hats in hot water; treat all affected household members

**Q9. Treatment of eyelash infestation (phthiriasis palpebrarum).**
- Occlusive petrolatum twice daily for 8–10 days, mechanical removal, or oral ivermectin; pediculicides not used near the eyes

**Q10. Why is lindane no longer used?**
- Neurotoxicity (seizures) especially in children and with misuse; banned/withdrawn in many countries including India (please confirm current status)

**Q11. Causes of treatment failure?**
- Resistance (kdr mutations to permethrin), wrong application, reinfestation from untreated contacts, no second application, misdiagnosis of dead nits as active infestation

## Quick spotter facts
- Nits firmly cemented on one side of hair shaft
- Maculae caeruleae — pubic lice
- Body louse — vector of epidemic typhus, trench fever, relapsing fever

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Infestations). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
